title: Getting started: your first campaign
description: Create your first campaign, connect a traffic source, point it at an offer and read your first reconciled conversion in minutes.
text: What you are building A tracker records one row per click and joins the conversions that come back to it later. To get that first row you need three things: a traffic source to label where the click came from, an offer to send the visitor to, and a campaign that ties the two together and hands you a link. Once that link is live, a click becomes a click, a postback becomes a conversion, and the ledger starts to reconcile. This walkthrough follows the shortest path to a working conversion. Everything else in the tracker — flows, landers, caps, splits — layers on top of these same three objects. Step 1 — Add the traffic source Open Manage → Traffic sources and pick your source from the presets, or add it from scratch. A traffic source stores the source's own click-id convention and the macros it understands, so the tracking link the tracker generates already carries the right placeholders. If your source is not in the list, add it and record how it passes a click id (for example a parameter such as click_id or a source-specific one). Get that wrong and the click still records — it just records without the identifier your source will quote back to you. Step 2 — Add the offer Open Manage → Offers and add the destination you are sending traffic to. Set the offer URL — the page the visitor lands on — and its payout. The offer URL accepts macros, and the one you will almost always use is {click_id} , which the tracker replaces with the click id it generated. Most networks need your click id in a parameter of their choosing. The tracker already appends click_id=… to the offer URL automatically, but the network usually reads a different name, so you add that name yourself in the offer's Target URL — for example &sub1={click_id} . Whatever the network calls it, that is the value it must echo back on the postback. Step 3 — Build the campaign Open Manage → Campaigns , create a campaign, and pick the traffic source and the offer you just made. Save it, then copy the campaign link. It takes the form: https://<your-domain>/<alias> The campaign link accepts a set of parameters when your source can pass them: click_id , cost , sub_id_1 through sub_id_10 , utm_* , external_id , and extras such as country or gender . Anything your source does not send is simply left empty. The alias is the short path you chose; it is what identifies the campaign when the link is clicked. Step 4 — Fire a test conversion There is no dedicated test-click or test-postback button. The honest test is the real path: fire a click on the campaign link, then send a postback for it by hand. Read the click id Open the campaign link in a browser. Then open Logs → Clicks and find the newest row. Copy its click id — that is the value the network would return to you. Send the postback On your own machine, replace the click id and hit the inbound postback endpoint. This is exactly what an affiliate network does when it reports a sale: curl "https://YOUR-TRACKER-DOMAIN/pb?clickid=YOUR-CLICK-ID&payout=25&status=sale" A good response is HTTP 200 with a body like {"status":"ok",…} . A 400 means the status or payout was rejected; a 403 means postback security blocked the call. The postback reference lists every accepted parameter and alias. Where to confirm everything Logs → Clicks — the click you fired, with its click id, sub-ids and UTM values. Logs → S2S postbacks — the inbound call you sent, including any rejection and its reason. Reports → Conversions — the conversion now attached to the click, where you can edit or delete it. When those three line up, the plumbing is finished. The next useful pages are Offers and offer URLs and Campaigns and flows , which is where routing and multiple offers come in. In-memory rehearsal A campaign row also has a Simulate action. It runs the flow, filter and cap logic in memory — side-effect free — without real traffic. Use it to sanity-check routing before you spend.

title: Rev-share offer with Meta traffic, end to end
description: Wire a rev-share offer to Meta traffic end to end: campaign link, postback, click id stitching and the conversion API.
text: What “rev-share with Meta” changes Two things make this setup different from a fixed-payout offer. A rev-share offer pays you a share of the sale value, and that share is almost never known when you paste the offer URL — it arrives with each conversion, on the postback. And with Meta you are buying the clicks yourself, so the click id has to survive from the ad click, through the network, and back to the tracker. This page wires both ends together. The rev-share consequence is simple: set the offer payout to 0 . The real amount comes back in the postback’s payout (or amount / sum ) field and accumulates on the conversion. If you leave a fixed payout on the offer you will over-report revenue before the network’s number lands. Step 1 — Add the affiliate network Open Manage → Networks → Add network , or start from the preset catalog (125 networks) so the record is pre-filled. A network stores the two things this walkthrough depends on: its own click-id convention (the parameter it will echo back, for example s1={click_id} or aff_sub={click_id} ) and its S2S postback template. If you add it by hand, type both in exactly as the network documents them. Step 2 — Hand the network the postback URL Open the network record’s S2S postback template and copy the URL into the network’s own conversion-tracking panel. The endpoint is: https://YOUR-TRACKER-DOMAIN/pb?clickid={clickid}&payout={payout}&status={status}&tid={tid} The preset template uses generic placeholders. The network’s panel fills macros of its own naming, so swap any placeholder the network names differently for that network’s token before you save. A payout macro called {sum} and a transaction macro called {txn} give a URL like: https://YOUR-TRACKER-DOMAIN/pb?clickid={clickid}&payout={sum}&status={status}&tid={txn} The parameter names on the left stay the tracker’s — or an accepted alias, since sum on its own is read as the payout name. Only the value macro changes to match what the network can fill. The full list of accepted names and what a good response looks like is on the postback reference ; to lock the endpoint down with a secret key and an IP allowlist, see Securing your postback URL . Step 3 — Add the offer with the network’s click-id parameter Open Manage → Offers → Add offer . Set the Target URL to the network’s offer URL and insert the network’s own click-id parameter with the {click_id} macro. If the network expects sub1 , that is: https://network.example.com/click?offer=123&sub1={click_id} The tracker already appends click_id=… to the offer URL automatically, but a network reads its own parameter, so you add that parameter yourself. The network record’s “Offer parameters” field is only a stored reference — it is not appended at runtime — so never rely on it to get the id onto the URL. Set Payout to 0 , pick the currency the network pays in, and leave the offer Active . The offers page details every field. Step 4 — Add the Meta traffic source Open Manage → Traffic sources → New from template and pick Meta. The preset captures fbclid from the ad URL automatically and stitches it with the _fbc and _fbp cookies — you do not map it. See Adding a traffic source if you would rather build it by hand. Step 5 — Create the campaign and copy the link Open Manage → Campaigns → Create campaign . Give it the Meta source and the offer, and run through the wizard. On the Settings step, set Ad-platform campaign ID to the Meta campaign’s id so spend can be matched later. Save, then copy the Campaign URL : https://<your-domain>/<alias> The link accepts click_id , cost , sub_id_1 … sub_id_10 , utm_* and external_id , so your Meta ad URL can carry the cost and any labels you want back. The wizard itself is covered in Campaigns and flows . Step 6 — Connect Meta CAPI and cost sync Two separate connections, both under Manage: CAPI — Manage → CAPI integrations , switch on Send conversions to Meta , then set the Dataset/Pixel ID and access token, a default currency and the statuses to send . Leave dry-run on to build and log the payload without sending, use Send test event to confirm the wiring, then turn dry-run off. Full detail: Sending conversions to Meta (CAPI) . Cost sync — Manage → Integrations , connect Meta. Spend is matched to a campaign by its Ad-platform campaign ID from Step 5. See Syncing Meta ad spend . Step 7 — Test it end to end There is no test-click or test-postback button. The honest test is the real path: Open the campaign link in a browser, optionally with ?cost=1.25 . Open Logs → Clicks , find the newest row and copy its click id . Send the postback by hand, exactly as the network will: curl "https://YOUR-TRACKER-DOMAIN/pb?clickid=YOUR-CLICK-ID&payout=12.50&status=sale" A {"status":"ok",…} body confirms the endpoint. Then open Logs → S2S postbacks for the inbound call, Reports → Conversions for the recorded sale, and Health centre to see the last successful postback. If nothing lands, Postback not recorded splits the 400, 403 and no-match cases. The two mistakes that cost the most First, leaving a fixed payout on the offer: with rev-share the payout must be 0 , because the money is whatever the postback says. Second, forgetting the network’s own click-id parameter on the Target URL — the auto-appended click_id=… is not the name the network reads, so the postback comes back with nothing to match.

title: Campaigns and flows
description: How campaigns hold your routing, targeting and caps, and how flows decide which offer or lander each visitor sees.
text: What a campaign is A campaign is your entry point for traffic. It ties a traffic source to the offers and landers you want to serve, and it hands you a public URL: https://<your-domain>/<alias> Open Manage → Campaigns → Create campaign and the editor runs as a three-step wizard: Settings · Targeting & rules · Postbacks & review . Only Name and Alias are required — every other field has a sensible default. Step 1 — Settings This step holds the campaign’s identity and its cost configuration. Field What it does Required Name Label shown in lists, pickers and reports. Yes Alias The short path that becomes the tracking link — /<alias> . Must be unique. Yes Type Campaign (runs flows) or Tracking only (records hits, no routing). No Status Active / paused switch. Paused campaigns stop serving. No Traffic source The source whose parameters and macro convention the link expects. No Domain Which of your tracking domains serves the link. No Flow selection Position (first matching flow wins) or Weight % (random split by weight, e.g. 70/30). Also shown as Distribution on step 2. No Tags Free-form labels for filtering the list. No Ad-platform campaign ID Ad-platform campaign id used by cost sync to match spend to this campaign. No Cost model CPC , CPUC , CPM , CPA , CPS , RevShare or Auto . No Traffic loss (%) Expected loss between the source’s reported clicks and tracked visits, kept for reconciliation. No Cost The cost value applied for the period. No Cost currency Currency the cost is recorded in. No There is also a Cost from cost parameter switch: when on, the per-click cost arriving on the campaign link wins over the fixed cost above. The alias is the only part of this step that changes the shape of your link, so pick it first. Step 2 — Targeting & rules This step defines the campaign’s flows . Each flow is a routing rule with its own target, filters, schedule, caps and weight: Flow type — forced flows are evaluated first, regular flows follow by position, and a default flow catches everything no other flow matched. Position / weight — used depending on whether Flow selection is Position or Weight % . Target — the offer, lander and/or campaign the flow serves. Filters — geo, device, traffic, sub-id/UTM and time conditions, combined with AND/OR and invertible with “IS NOT”. Schedule and caps — dayparting and per-hour / per-day / total click caps per flow. Direct vs multi flows and redirect modes A flow’s schema decides what the visitor gets. The ones you will use most: Schema What happens direct Redirects straight to the offer URL. Fastest path — no landing. landing_offer Serves a landing page; its click-out link then redirects to the offer. landing_only Serves a landing page with no offer click-out. multi Picks one landing and one offer at random from the configured pools (A/B rotation). redirect 302-redirects to a fixed URL. redirect_campaign Redirects the visitor into another campaign. return_404 Answers 404 — use as a “drop” flow for unwanted traffic. A complementary setting, Delivery action , controls how the destination is reached — 302 redirect (the default), iFrame , Form POST , Serve content or Do nothing . The Distribution control at the top of the step is the same choice as Flow selection in Settings. Step 3 — Postbacks & review The final step is where you tell the tracker what to send outbound when a conversion lands. Add a Postback URL , choose GET or POST , and tick which statuses should fire it. A traffic source also carries its own S2S postback URL with per-status toggles, and this campaign step lets you add campaign-specific ones. The review pane below summarizes the name, alias, cost model and postback count before you Save . Note the direction: inbound postbacks (the network reporting a sale to you) go to /pb and are not configured here — see the postback reference . This step is the tracker reporting onward to your source. Simulate before you spend A campaign row has a Simulate action. It runs the flow, filter, schedule and cap logic in memory — side-effect free, no redirects and no postbacks — and returns how the traffic would be distributed. Use it to confirm the routing before real visitors arrive. You can pin a country, device, OS or IP prefix for the run. Two different “modes” people mix up Flow selection / Distribution decides which flow is chosen (first match vs weighted split). A flow’s schema decides what that flow does (direct to offer, through a lander, multi rotation). One is the selector; the other is the destination. Setting one does not change the other.

title: Server-to-server postbacks: the complete reference
description: The inbound postback URL, every accepted parameter alias, default statuses, de-duplication and the exact responses you get back.
text: The inbound URL A server-to-server (S2S) postback is how your affiliate network tells the tracker that a conversion happened. The network calls a URL on your tracker domain; the tracker records the conversion against the click and answers. The endpoint is: https://YOUR-TRACKER-DOMAIN/pb?clickid={clickid}&payout={payout}&status={status}&tid={tid} The four parameters above are the ones a network's postback template usually fills. Only the click id is really the point of the call — see the defaults below for what happens when the rest are empty. The endpoint accepts GET , POST and HEAD . If a network is configured with the older path form of the URL, that form redirects to this query form, so existing templates keep working. Give each network the URL in the shape it expects to fill. If your tracker is on your own domain, copy the postback URL straight out of the network's conversion-tracking settings after you have saved it. Accepted parameters and aliases Parameter names are matched case-insensitively and the first non-empty value wins. That means a network that calls the status type and another that calls it event can both post to the same URL without changes. Meaning Accepted names (first non-empty wins) Click id click_id , clickid , click , subid , sub_id , cid Status status , type , event , conversion_type Payout payout , sum , amount , revenue , price Transaction tid , transaction_id , external_id , txn , transactionid The tracker also accepts pass-through values sub_id_1 through sub_id_10 , external_id and transaction_id — they are stored on the conversion for reporting and for attribution fallbacks. Defaults when a field is missing A missing status is recorded as lead . A missing payout is recorded as 0 . There is no currency parameter on /pb . The currency a conversion is recorded in comes from the offer or the workspace, not from the postback. Built-in statuses are lead , sale , upsale , rejected , hold and trash . Custom statuses can be defined in Settings, and an unknown status is rejected rather than stored. What happens to revenue and status Repeat postbacks for the same click accumulate payout and revenue — this is how lifetime value builds up over several conversions — while the recorded status reflects the latest call. So a click that first reports lead and later reports sale ends up as a sale, with both amounts added together. Duplicates are guarded. A repeat carrying the same transaction id , or an identical anonymous status + payout inside roughly a 60-second window, only bumps the postback counter; revenue is not added a second time. A duplicate call is still a success from the network's point of view. Attribution and the clickless path The ideal postback carries the click id the tracker generated. When it cannot be matched, the tracker falls back in order: match on the transaction id , then match on unique sub-ids inside an attribution window, then record an unattributed row so the conversion is not lost. An unattributed row still appears in reports and can be re-attributed later from the conversion log. The clickless conversions page covers the import path and the window in more detail. Responses Response Meaning 200 {"status":"ok",…} The conversion was accepted and recorded. 200 {"status":"rejected",…} A rule blocked the conversion, but the call was understood. 400 Invalid status, or a non-numeric payout. 403 Postback security denied the call — bad or missing key, or an IP outside the allowlist. Securing the endpoint /pb is public by design — any network you work with has to reach it. You can require proof with a secret key, passed as ?key= , ?secret= , or the X-Postback-Key header, and optionally restrict callers to an IP allowlist (comma-separated IPs or CIDR ranges). Both are configured in Settings → Postback security . A call that fails either check gets the 403 above. See Securing your postback URL . Confirming what arrived Logs → S2S postbacks shows inbound calls as they land, including rejections and their reason. Reports → Conversions is where the recorded conversion can be edited or deleted. Health centre shows the last successful postback per source, which tells you quickly whether a network has gone quiet. If nothing lands Work through Postback not recorded : it splits the problem into the 400 and 403 cases and the case where the click id simply does not match.

title: Click IDs and URL macros
description: How click ids travel from the campaign link to the network and back, and the macros you can drop into an offer URL.
text: What a click id is Every click the tracker records gets a click id — a unique value generated at the moment of the click. It is the thread that ties a click to the conversion that arrives later: the offer URL carries it out, the network echoes it back on the postback, and the tracker joins the two. Get the click id round the loop intact and attribution is exact; lose it and the tracker has to fall back to a less certain match. The click-id lifecycle Generated at the click. When a visitor hits the campaign link https:/// , the tracker generates a click id — unless the link already carried one in click_id , in which case that value wins and is kept. Passed to the offer. At click-out the tracker substitutes {click_id} in the offer URL wherever it appears, and always appends click_id=… to the final URL. Handed to the network in its own parameter. Most networks ignore click_id and read a name of their own choosing, so you add it to the offer's Target URL — for example &sub1={click_id} or &aff_sub={click_id} . Returned on the postback. The network calls /pb with the value in a click-id alias such as clickid , subid or cid , and the tracker matches it back to the click. The offer-parameters field is a stored reference An affiliate network record has an Offer parameters field that stores that network's click-id convention (for example s1={click_id} ). It is documentation you keep next to the network — it is not appended to your offers at runtime . The macro has to live in the offer's own Target URL for the network to receive it. See Offers and offer URLs and Adding an affiliate network for where each piece is entered. The sub-id chain sub_id_1 through sub_id_10 are ten free slots for values your traffic source passes on the campaign link — ad set, creative, keyword, placement, anything. The tracker stores them on the click and exposes them as offer macros, so you can forward the ones the network should see (for example &s2={sub_id_2} ), and the network can echo them back on the postback as passthrough fields. That chain is what lets a report split revenue by the source's own granularity, and it is the fallback key when a clickless conversion has no transaction id. What the campaign link accepts Parameter Purpose click_id The source's own click id; kept instead of generating a new one. cost Per-click cost for this hit. sub_id_1 … sub_id_10 Your own identifiers, carried end to end. utm_source , utm_medium , utm_campaign Campaign tagging; other utm_* values are collected too. external_id The source's own entity id (ad, ad set). country , region , city , gender Extra attributes some sources append. Anything the source does not send is simply left empty. If a source uses different names, map its token to the canonical one in that source's paramsIdMapping (for example clickid → click ) — see Adding a traffic source . Offer URL macros Place a macro in single braces anywhere in the offer URL; the tracker replaces it with the value from the current hit. Unknown macros are left exactly as written , so a typo shows up in the URL rather than silently blanking it. Macro Value {click_id} The click's unique id {sub_id_1} … {sub_id_10} Sub-ids 1–10 {external_id} External (ad) id {visitor_id} First-party visitor id, stable across sessions {country} {region} {city} Geo {ip} {isp} {connection_type} Network and connection {os} {os_version} Operating system {browser} {browser_version} Browser {device_type} {device_brand} {device_model} Device {language} Visitor locale {referrer} {keyword} Referrer and search keyword {cost} {currency} Click cost and its currency {utm_source} {utm_medium} {utm_campaign} {utm_creative} UTM tags carried by the hit {offer_id} {campaign_id} {landing_id} Tracker object ids {payout} The offer's payout {_md5} MD5 hex of the click id {_md5} {_md5} is the MD5 hex digest of the click id — a fixed-length, opaque version of the same value. Use it when a network wants a hashed or length-limited identifier, or when you want a deterministic token that cannot be traced back to the raw id. The same click id always produces the same {_md5} , so it works as a stable join key on the network's side too. Lander and fallback macros Inside a local lander's HTML, the placeholder {offer} is replaced with the click-out URL /c/{alias}/{offer_id} , so a button like Continue always routes back through the tracker. A campaign's Fallback URL (and the workspace-wide fallback) accepts the same click macros as an offer URL, plus {campaign_name} and {_md5} — useful when the drop-off page needs to know which campaign sent the visitor. Outgoing postback tokens The outbound postback the tracker sends to a traffic source or on a campaign cycle supports everything in the offer macro table, plus the conversion-specific tokens below. These belong in a source's S2S postback URL, not in an offer URL. Token Value {payout} The conversion payout being reported {revenue} {profit} Revenue and profit for the row {status} {status2} Primary status, and a secondary status when the row carries one {_md5} MD5 hex of the click id {unixconversiontime} Conversion time as Unix epoch seconds event_1 … event_30 Custom conversion event parameters A literal payout=auto in a postback URL is replaced with the payout actually being fired, so one template can serve offers with different payouts. Unknown tokens in a postback URL stay literal; a known token with no value resolves to empty. Geo, device and UTM values Geo and device macros are filled from what the tracking request resolves — the visitor's IP, User-Agent and any proxy/CDN geo header — so they are available even when the source sends nothing. UTM macros come from the UTM parameters on the hit. Where a value could not be resolved, the macro is simply empty rather than guessed; that is the honest result, but it also means a report grouped by {city} will be sparse if your source never passes usable location data. Keep the id in one place The tracker appends click_id=… to every offer URL on its own, so the network parameter you add (for example &sub1={click_id} ) is the only extra one it needs. Give the same parameter name to the network's postback template so what goes out comes back.

title: Clickless conversions and manual import
description: Record conversions without a click id using a transaction id or unique sub-ids, and import a batch of conversions from a file.
text: When a conversion has no click id A clickless conversion is one that arrives without the click id the tracker generated. It happens more often than people expect: a call centre closes a sale hours later, a CRM batches approvals overnight, or a network's postback simply does not echo the value you sent. The tracker's rule is that a conversion is never dropped — it is matched to the best available evidence, and if none of it is decisive the row is still kept. The matching ladder Matching runs in order and stops at the first confident hit: Transaction id. A repeat transaction_id (or external_id ) updates the same row, so a re-delivered sale counts once. Unique sub-ids. Sub-ids 1–5 are compared against real clicks inside the workspace attribution window (default 7 days ). The match must be unique — exactly one click — otherwise the tracker refuses to guess. The visitor. The first-party visitor id ( aaa_vid ) is stitched to that visitor's latest click (last-click) or earliest click (first-click), according to Settings → Attribution, again inside the window. Unattributed. If nothing resolves, the row is written with click id none : visible in reports, still editable, and re-attributable later. Uniqueness is the safeguard A shared sub-id is not enough. If two clicks match the same sub-ids, the tracker will not merge two customers — the conversion stays unattributed until you attach it by hand. That is deliberate: a wrong match is worse than no match. Offline / phone ingestion API For CRMs, call centres and other server-side systems, post the conversion to the ingestion endpoint. It takes a workspace API token as a Bearer header (or an admin session) and accepts a JSON object or a form-encoded body: POST /backend/api/reports/ingest Authorization: Bearer <api-token> { "click_id": "9f2c1a7e-…", "status": "sale", "payout": 42.5, "transaction_id": "CRM-10432", "currency": "EUR", "occurred_at": "2026-10-05T14:02:00Z", "sub_id_1": "campaign-a" } The fields it understands: Field Notes click_id Optional if another key is supplied. status Defaults to sale when omitted; built-in or custom statuses accepted. payout Plain number; a non-numeric value is rejected. transaction_id / external_id The idempotency key — re-sending the same value updates the existing row. currency Accepted here; unlike /pb , which has no currency parameter. occurred_at ISO-8601 timestamp of the real conversion. sub_id_1 … sub_id_10 Match keys and reporting dimensions. phone , note Stored on the conversion history. A valid call answers with a JSON result such as {"result":"created","attributed":true,…} or {"result":"updated",…} for a repeat; a bad payload gets a clear rejected reason rather than an error page. The endpoint matches click id, external id or transaction id first, then falls back to unique sub-ids inside the attribution window, exactly like the postback path. Importing a batch from a file Reports → Conversions → Import conversions takes a CSV-style list, one conversion per line: click_id,payout,transaction_id,status An existing click id accumulates onto its row; an unknown id creates an unattributed row rather than being discarded. The importer also accepts optional occurred_at and currency columns, and the status may be any built-in or custom status. Which path to use Situation Use Network reports a sale in real time Its S2S postback to /pb — see the postback reference . Call centre or CRM closes offline orders POST /backend/api/reports/ingest , from the system that owns the order. A partner emails a spreadsheet The Import conversions dialog in Reports → Conversions. A thank-you page with no server callback The conversion pixel or JS snippet — see Conversion pixel and JS tracking . Why the currency note matters Inbound /pb deliberately has no currency parameter — a conversion's currency comes from the offer or the workspace. The ingestion API and the CSV importer, by contrast, do accept a currency , because an offline order knows the currency it was sold in. If you are moving data from a CRM and the total is coming out in the wrong unit, check that the currency was sent on the ingestion call rather than assumed from the offer. Confirming and fixing the result Reports → Conversions lists every row, attributed or not; filter or edit to attach an unattributed conversion to the right click. Logs → Conversions shows the history and the source of each event. Health centre and the reports you already watch will show an unattributed spike if a feed starts sending bad keys. Send the strongest key you have A transaction id resolves instantly and idempotently. Sub-ids and the visitor id are fallbacks, not substitutes — they can match several clicks and then be refused. When a CRM can send both a transaction id and a click id, send both.

title: Conversion pixel and JS tracking
description: Client-side conversion tracking with the pixel and JavaScript snippet, and when to prefer server-to-server instead.
text: Server callback or browser callback Most conversion data should arrive server to server: the network or your CRM calls the tracker directly, which does not depend on the visitor's browser and cannot be blocked by it. There are two cases, though, where no server callback exists — a thank-you page on a destination you do not control, or a client-side event such as a form submit — and that is what the conversion pixel and the JavaScript snippet are for. This page covers both, and the postback reference covers the server path. Direct JS tracking Add the snippet to any page on your own site: The script keeps a first-party visitor id in the aaa_cid cookie (with a localStorage copy, 30 days), then posts a visit to /t/collect using sendBeacon , falling back to fetch and finally an image request. The visit is recorded as a visit, not a click, and the response is {"status":"ok","click_id":"…"} . Once the script is loaded it exposes three functions: Function What it does aaaTrack() Returns the visitor's click id (and fires the collect). aaaClickThrough(url) Appends &click_id= to a click-out URL so /c/{alias}/{offer} reuses the same id. aaaFire(status, payout, extra) Fires a client-side conversion pixel for this visitor. /t/collect also works on its own as a GET or POST with ?c={alias}&click_id=… . It collects UTM parameters and the page title, honours bot rules (blocked bots get a 404) and respects the GDPR opt-out cookie. The conversion pixel The pixel is a single request that records a conversion and returns a 1×1 GIF: GET /p/{alias}?click_id=9f2c1a7e&status=sale&payout=10.5 The click id comes from ?click_id= or, when the snippet is present, from the aaa_cid cookie it set. Extra attribution fields — transaction_id , external_id and sub_id_1 through sub_id_10 — pass through as query parameters. A bare pixel with no click id and no attribution parameters gets a 400 , and an opted-out visitor gets the GIF with nothing recorded. Because it is addressed by campaign alias, the pixel is bound to one campaign. How the click id is carried through The visit lands and /t.js writes the visitor's click id to the aaa_cid cookie. aaaClickThrough(url) appends click_id=… to the click-out so the offer click reuses the same id rather than minting a new one. On the thank-you page the pixel reads ?click_id=… first and falls back to the cookie, so you get the same id without wiring anything. If you do not use the snippet, pass the click id to the pixel yourself in the URL. If neither the URL nor the cookie has an id, supply a transaction id or sub-id and the pixel takes the clickless path . Pixel or snippet? Situation Use A thank-you page you host, no server callback The pixel with ?click_id=… , or aaaFire() if the snippet is already on the page. You want every page view tracked, plus a conversion later The JS snippet — it sets the cookie and exposes the API. A destination page you do not control The pixel: paste one tag with its click id hard-coded, or render the URL server-side. The conversion happens on a server you own Prefer S2S — see postbacks and offline ingestion . JSON-mode pixel Add &fmt=json to get a JSON response instead of a GIF: curl "https://your-domain.com/p/my-campaign?click_id=9f2c1a7e&status=lead&payout=3.25&fmt=json" This is the right form when the call is made by script or by a server rather than by a browser image tag, because you can read the result — for example to confirm the conversion was recorded or to surface an invalid status. The GIF form is for embedding on a page, where nothing reads the response. Cross-domain and impressions The pixel and /t.js are served with open CORS headers so they work from any domain, which is what lets you track a destination page you do not host. There is also an impression pixel, GET /i/{alias} , which records an impression and returns a 1×1 GIF so view-through reporting can attribute a later conversion through the same aaa_cid cookie. Testing a pixel by hand There is no test button. Fire a click on the campaign link, copy the click id from Logs → Clicks , then call /p (or /pb ) with curl and &fmt=json . Confirm the conversion in Reports → Conversions . That exercises the same path the browser would. Browser tracking can be blocked Ad blockers, ITP and disabled cookies can stop a pixel or script from firing. Treat browser tracking as a convenience for pages with no server callback; treat the server-to-server postback or the ingestion API as the dependable path for money-critical conversions.

title: Cost models and cost handling
description: Cost models, when a cost is recorded, and how to send cost and currency on the campaign link or sync it from an ad platform.
text: Cost, revenue and profit A tracker holds two sides of a ledger. Revenue is what a conversion is worth — it arrives on an inbound postback and accumulates over the life of a click. Cost is what you paid to get that visitor — it is recorded once, at click time, from the traffic source or from an ad platform. Everything else in reporting is derived from those two numbers: profit = revenue − cost ROI % = (revenue − cost) / cost × 100 EPC = revenue / clicks Get cost wrong and every ROI figure is wrong with it, which is why the cost model and the cost parameter matter as much as the offer payout does. The cost models A campaign carries a Cost model — the billing basis it is bought on. Choose it under Manage → Campaigns → Add/Edit campaign , in the Costs section. Model The campaign is billed per CPC Click (cost per click). CPUC Unique click (cost per unique click). CPM Thousand impressions (cost per mille). CPA Acquisition — a fixed amount per conversion. CPS Sale — a fixed amount per sale. RevShare Share of the revenue the traffic produced. Auto No fixed basis; let cost arrive from the parameter or the sync. The model records how the campaign is bought so reports and teammates can read it. Whatever model you pick, the spend that actually lands on a click arrives through one of the three paths below. Entering cost on a campaign The Costs section of the campaign editor holds all of the cost settings together: Field What it does Cost model The billing basis, from the table above. Traffic loss (%) The expected gap between the clicks the source reports and the visits the tracker records, kept for reconciliation. Cost A campaign-level cost value. Used for the whole period when no per-click cost arrives. Cost currency The currency that Cost value is expressed in. Cost from cost parameter When on, the cost value passed on each click is used instead of the flat campaign Cost. The cost query parameter Most traffic sources can pass the price of a click straight through. The campaign link accepts a cost parameter alongside the usual identifiers: https://<your-domain>/<alias>?cost=0.45&sub_id_1=adset-42 The value is stored on the click itself, so per-click cost can vary by placement, keyword or time of day. For the tracker to read it, map the source's own token to the cost parameter in the source's Settings mapping — for example a token of {cost} on the row whose Parameter is cost . If nothing maps, the parameter is ignored. Traffic loss Traffic loss is a percentage, not a deduction. It records the expected difference between the clicks a source bills you for and the visits that reach the tracker — redirects that fail, ad blockers, dropped requests. It is stored per campaign and per source so a reconciliation discrepancy can be explained rather than merely seen. It does not change the recorded cost; it is context for reading it. Ad-platform cost sync If you advertise on an ad platform, you can let the platform's reported spend become your cost automatically. The campaign's Ad-platform campaign ID field (in the campaign editor) is what ties the two records together. Connect the platform under Manage → Integrations and pick the ad accounts to read. On each campaign, set Ad-platform campaign ID so spend can be matched to it. The sync pulls each day's spend and impressions, then writes cost onto that day's clicks — the per-click cost is the day's spend divided by that day's clicks. It is idempotent: re-running a sync replaces the day's allocation rather than adding to it, so running it twice never doubles your spend. Spend for a campaign with no clicks that day is stored but allocates nothing. Use Test mode (dry-run) to compute and log the numbers without changing any costs. The full walkthrough is in Syncing Meta ad spend . Retroactive cost update Sometimes the number is simply wrong and you want to overwrite it. In Reports , the Cost update action opens a Retroactive cost update dialog: Field Meaning Campaign Optional. Leave empty to apply to all campaigns. From / To The date range to overwrite. Cost per click The value written onto every matching row. Total spend becomes cost × matched rows. Every applied change is recorded in Logs → Cost updates , so you can see what was overwritten and when. The usual mistake Cost defaults to 0 until one of the three paths supplies it. A campaign with a cost model but no per-click cost , no campaign Cost value and no sync reports 100% ROI on every conversion. If profit looks impossibly good, check cost first — see Cost is missing or wrong .

title: Adding a traffic source
description: Add a traffic source, capture its click-id convention, and generate a tracking link with that source's real macros.
text: What a traffic source is A traffic source is the record of where your clicks come from. It holds the source's own click-id convention, the macros it understands, where conversion data should be sent back to it, and the expected traffic loss. A campaign always points at one source, and that source is what lets the tracker name the channel behind every click. The catalog and "New from template" Open Manage → Sources . The catalog ships around 187 presets , each with the source's real pass-through macros filled in. New from template opens the catalog; Add source opens a blank form. In the catalog you can search sources, and filter to All or With API integrations . A preset carries capability badges for the automation it supports: Badge Meaning cost Cost update supported. pause_campaign Campaign pausing supported. blacklist Blacklisting supported. pause_creative Creative pausing supported. A preset with no badges is marked No API integration — it still tracks clicks, it just cannot be driven by the automation the badges describe. If your source is not in the list, use Add source and fill in the same fields by hand. The fields Field What it does Source name The label used everywhere the source appears — reports, filters, the campaign picker. Traffic loss (%) The expected gap between the clicks the source reports and the visits tracked here, kept for reconciliation. S2S postback URL Where the tracker sends conversion data to the source (outbound — see below). S2S postback statuses Checkboxes for sale , lead , rejected and upsale , choosing which statuses fire the outbound postback. Conversion fanout controls Two switches that thin out what the source is told — see below. Additional settings Free-form key/value pairs for the source integration, such as API keys. Settings mapping Rows of Name / Parameter / Token mapping the source's macros to tracker parameters. The S2S postback URL here is outbound Read this one carefully, because the same phrase means the opposite thing in the two records. On a traffic source , the S2S postback URL is outbound : it is the URL on the source's side that the tracker calls when a conversion lands. The tracker fills the placeholders with real values, for example: https://source.example.com/post?clickid={click_id}&payout={payout}&status={status} The source's postback template is not your tracker's /pb endpoint. On an affiliate network , the S2S postback URL is the inbound template you hand to the network so it can call you — that is covered in Adding an affiliate network and the postback reference . Do not paste your own postback URL here If you paste https://YOUR-TRACKER-DOMAIN/pb… into a source's outbound field, the tracker will call itself on every conversion. Use the URL the source gave you for receiving postbacks. S2S postback statuses The four checkboxes decide which conversion statuses are worth telling the source about. Tick sale and lead for the common case; add rejected if the source wants to know about reversals, and upsale if it pays on them. A status left unticked simply does not fire an outbound postback. Conversion fanout controls Don't forward upsell conversions to this source — sale and lead forwards are unaffected, and campaign postbacks are unaffected. Use it when the source only wants the first conversion. Forward only this share of conversions (%) — leave empty to forward every conversion. The same click id always gets the same decision, so a source sees a consistent sample rather than a random flicker. Settings mapping Each row maps one value. Name is the human label, Parameter is the tracker parameter it lands in, and Token is the source's macro that fills it. For example, the Cost row maps a token of {cost} to the cost parameter so per-click spend is captured; {campaign_id} maps to utm_campaign . Mapped values flow into reports, filters, macros and postbacks. This mapping is also how the source's click id is captured — for example a token such as clickid on the row whose Parameter is click_id . Meta needs no click-id mapping Meta's fbclid is captured automatically from the ad URL and stitched with the _fbc and _fbp cookies. You do not map it, and you do not need a token for it. To push conversions back to Meta, see Sending conversions to Meta (CAPI) . Confirming it works Health centre shows the last successful postback per source, which tells you quickly whether an outbound destination has gone quiet. Logs → Internal postbacks shows the outbound delivery attempts this tracker sent, with their outcome. Reports breaks any metric down by traffic source once clicks are flowing.

title: Adding an affiliate network
description: Add an affiliate network, store its click-id parameter and postback template, and give it the URL it needs to call back.
text: What an affiliate network is An affiliate network is the party that pays you for a conversion. It groups your offers, stores the click-id convention the network expects, and holds the postback template the network will call. An offer points at a network; a campaign does not, so the same network record can sit behind many offers. The catalog and "From catalog" Open Manage → Networks . The catalog ships around 125 presets , each with the network's click-id parameter and its standard postback template pre-filled. From catalog opens it; Add affiliate network opens a blank form. In the catalog you can search by network name or vertical, and narrow by vertical chips (Dating, Gambling, Nutra, Sweepstakes, and others). Once added, a preset network is marked as a Preset and can still be edited like any other. The catalog can also be opened from the offer editor: the Affiliate network picker has a + button that creates a network without leaving the offer form. The fields Field What it does Network name The label used in the offer's network picker and in filtering. Offer parameters A stored reference recording the network's click-id convention, e.g. s1={click_id} or subid={click_id} . Comma or JSON format. S2S postback URL The inbound template you hand to the network, so its conversions land in your tracker. Offer parameters is a stored reference This is the field readers get wrong. Offer parameters is not appended to your offer URL at runtime. It is a note-to-self: it records what the network calls your click-id parameter, so you know what to write when you build the offer's Target URL. The tracker already appends click_id=… to every offer URL automatically, but a network almost always reads the id under its own name. You add that yourself in the offer's Target URL . If the network's Offer parameters say s1={click_id} , then the offer URL gets: https://network.example.com/offer?aff=12345&s1={click_id} At click-out, {click_id} is replaced with the tracker-generated id, and the network echoes it back on the postback. Repeat that for any extra fields the network wants, such as &s2={sub_id_1} . The full macro list and the click-id round trip are covered in Offers and offer URLs and Click IDs and URL macros . The click id must be in the offer's Target URL Writing s1={click_id} into Offer parameters does nothing by itself. If you never place &s1={click_id} in the offer's Target URL, the network never receives your click id — the click still records, but the conversion comes back with nothing to match it to. See Postback not recorded . The S2S postback URL is the template you hand over On a network, the S2S postback URL is inbound : it is a URL on your tracker that the network calls when a conversion happens. The preset fills it with the standard template: https://YOUR-TRACKER-DOMAIN/pb?clickid={clickid}&payout={payout}&status={status}&tid={tid} Replace YOUR-TRACKER-DOMAIN with your tracker domain and paste the result into the network's own conversion-tracking settings. The braces are the network's macros — it substitutes its real click id and payout when it calls you. This is the opposite direction from a traffic source 's postback URL, which is outbound. The accepted parameters, aliases, defaults and responses are all in the postback reference . Same URL, network's own macro names The template above uses {clickid} , {payout} , {status} and {tid} because those are common network macro names. The tracker accepts those aliases case-insensitively, so you rarely need to change the template — just paste it where the network asks for its postback URL. Confirming it works Logs → S2S postbacks shows inbound calls from the network as they arrive, including any rejection and its reason. Reports → Conversions is where a recorded conversion can be inspected, edited or deleted. Health centre shows whether postbacks are landing, which is the quickest signal that the network has gone quiet.

title: Offers and offer URLs
description: Build an offer URL, place macros where the network expects the click id, and manage payouts and currencies per offer.
text: What an offer is An offer is the final destination of a click — the network’s page the visitor is sent to. Open Manage → Offers → Add offer to create one. The wizard is a short form; this page walks every field, then explains the one thing most people get wrong: getting your click id onto the network’s URL. Every field Field What it does Offer name Label shown in lists, pickers and reports. Use the network’s offer id in the name so you can find it fast. Target URL The page the visitor lands on. Accepts macros; the network’s click-id parameter must be placed here (see below). Affiliate network The network this offer belongs to, so its click-id convention and postback template are known. Countries ISO-code targeting list — search by name or code. Leave empty for all countries. Payout The value a conversion is worth, in this offer’s currency. Set 0 for a rev-share offer. Currency The currency the payout (and the postback’s amount) is recorded in. Status Active, paused or archived. Archiving is a soft delete — restore any time. Daily conversions cap Stop serving the offer once this many conversions land in a day; traffic overflows to the Overflow offer . Overflow offer Where traffic goes when the daily cap is reached. Below the main fields there are also Tags (free-form, e.g. nutra , tier1 ), Notes and an optional CAPI pixel binding. Offers can be created in bulk with a CSV whose header is id,name,url,affiliate_network_id,countries,payout,currency,status,tags,daily_conversions_cap,overflow_offer_id,notes . Putting the network’s click id into the Target URL When a click-out happens, the tracker substitutes every {macro} in the Target URL from the click’s data and also appends click_id=… automatically. That auto-append is not enough on its own: a network reads its own parameter name, and if that parameter is not on the URL the network has nothing to echo back on the postback. Your conversion arrives with an empty or wrong click id. The fix is to insert the network’s parameter into the Target URL with the {click_id} macro. If the network expects sub1 , the URL becomes: https://network.example.com/click?offer=123&sub1={click_id} Other networks use different names — s1={click_id} , aff_sub={click_id} , and so on. Use whichever the network documents. One caution: the “Offer parameters” field on the network record is a stored reference only. It is not appended to the offer URL at runtime, so the parameter has to live on the Target URL itself. Offer URL macros Placeholders are single-brace; unknown macros are left untouched. The ones you will reach for most: Macro Value Macro Value {click_id} Unique click id {visitor_id} First-party visitor id {sub_id_1} … {sub_id_10} Sub ids 1–10 {offer_id} / {campaign_id} Offer / campaign id {country} / {city} / {region} Geo {os} / {browser} / {device_type} Device & platform {language} Locale {referrer} / {keyword} Context {cost} / {currency} Click cost & currency {ip} / {isp} Network details {utm_*} UTM tags {_md5} / {payout} Hashed value / payout The full set also includes {device_brand} , {os_version} , {browser_version} , {connection_type} and {landing_id} . Local landing files use {offer} for the click-out URL. See Click IDs and URL macros for how the id travels end to end. Rev-share offers With a rev-share deal the amount you are paid is a share of the sale, so it cannot be known when you build the offer. Set Payout to 0 and let the value come in on the postback’s payout (or amount / sum ) field. The tracker accumulates that amount onto the conversion, and repeats for the same click add up — that is how lifetime value builds. Set the Currency to match what the network pays, because the postback itself carries no currency parameter. Daily caps and overflow Daily conversions cap counts conversions per day for the offer. Once it is reached the offer stops taking new traffic, and any click that would have gone to it is sent to the Overflow offer instead. Set the cap as a whole number; leave it empty or 0 for unlimited. If the cap is hit and no overflow offer is configured, the offers flow simply stops matching and normal campaign fallback applies. The one that breaks postbacks Never assume the auto-appended click_id=… is enough. Check the offer’s Target URL carries the network’s own parameter with the {click_id} macro — for example &sub1={click_id} . Without it, conversions land unattributed and look like they were never tracked.

title: Sending conversions to Meta (CAPI)
description: Send conversions to Meta server-side from Manage → CAPI integrations, with the statuses to send, a default currency and a dry-run.
text: What the conversion API does The Meta Conversions API (CAPI) sends your conversions from the tracker's server straight to Meta, independent of the browser — so they survive ad blockers, browser restrictions and the drop in third-party cookies. Meta matches each event back to the ad click using the click identifiers the tracker captured (see below), not the tracker's own click id: a click that arrived with fbclid= is what makes a match possible. Everything lives on Manage → CAPI integrations — open the Meta tile and press Manage all to see its pixels. Meta is the only platform whose sender is live today; the other tiles store records but send nothing yet. Turning it on On Manage → CAPI integrations , open the Meta tile. Switch on Send conversions to Meta . Set the dataset and token — either the fallback fields or one or more pixel records (below). Leave Dry-run on and use Send test event while testing, then clear the test event code and turn dry-run off. Press Save settings — it stays disabled until the stored settings load, so a failed load cannot overwrite your configuration with the page defaults. Fallback dataset versus pixel records There are two ways to tell the tracker where to send: Where Fields When it is used Fallback (on the Meta panel) Fallback Dataset / Pixel ID and Fallback access token Only when no pixel is bound. The token is stored as a secret. Pixel records (Add new pixel) Pixel / Dataset ID , API key / Access token , plus the per-pixel options below When bound to a traffic channel or an offer. A pixel's own id and token win. Bind a pixel in one place: at the traffic-channel level to send only that channel's conversions, or at the offer / website level to send all of that offer's conversions from any channel. If it is bound at both levels, the sender resolves the channel first and still sends once, so this is redundant rather than harmful. The access token and the test event code The access token authenticates the call. Treat it as a secret: masked and stored hidden, and it must belong to the same dataset as the id beside it. A mismatched pair fails at Meta and appears in Logs → Internal postbacks as a failed send with Meta's error text. Test event code is optional. With it filled in, every event is routed to the Test Events tab of Meta's Events Manager instead of the normal stream — useful for confirming the wiring, but those events do not count as conversions in ad reporting. Clear it when you go live. Which conversion statuses to send The Send these conversion statuses checkboxes control what leaves the tracker. Defaults are lead , sale and upsale ; custom statuses you defined also appear. A status that is not ticked is skipped silently — no event, and no row in the outbound log. Each status maps to a Meta event name: defaults are sale → Purchase , lead → Lead and upsale → Subscribe . With a pixel record, the pixel's Default event name applies to every status unless a Custom conversion matching row overrides it. Currency and value The event's value is the conversion payout; its currency is the conversion's own, falling back to the panel's Default currency (USD, EUR, GBP or JPY). A pixel can carry payout customisations — one row per conversion type with a fixed Value and/or Currency that overrides those defaults. Leave both empty to keep the conversion's numbers. fbclid, _fbc and _fbp are captured for you You do not map Meta's click identifiers. On a Meta ad click the tracker reads fbclid from the ad URL automatically and stitches it with the _fbc and _fbp cookies: fbp comes from the _fbp cookie. fbc uses the _fbc cookie when present; otherwise it is derived from fbclid in Meta's required form fb.1.<unix-ms>.<fbclid> . Those values are stored on the click and carried into the event's user_data , along with the visitor's IP and user agent. With Include hashed email/phone when the postback provides them on, any email or phone on the conversion is normalised and SHA-256 hashed before sending. If a redirect, landing page or URL builder strips the query string, the click arrives without fbclid and Meta has little to match on — check that first when conversions do not appear. Per-pixel overrides A pixel record can be tuned beyond its id and token: Field What it does Default event name The Meta event used for every conversion this pixel receives unless a custom match overrides it. Event URL Optional event_source_url sent with the event. Action source Store tracking URL, App, Offline, Chat or Other. Data Quality API Token Optional; stored as a secret. Status active or inactive . Custom conversion matching Maps a conversion type to a specific Meta event name; anything not listed uses the default event name. Dry-run and Send test event Dry-run (build + log the payload, send nothing) is on by default : the payload is built and the outcome recorded, but no HTTP call is made. Send test event saves the settings, then sends one synthetic event so you can confirm credentials and formatting; the result is shown on the page. Turn dry-run off only when you are ready for real events to reach Meta. The two silent failures Dry-run left on, and a status that is not ticked. Both write no row to Logs → Internal postbacks , so the sender looks broken when it is simply not running. Confirm those two first, then follow Meta shows no conversions in order. Cost is a separate connection: Syncing Meta ad spend pulls your spend in and matches it to the campaign.

title: Syncing Meta ad spend
description: Connect Meta under Manage → Integrations and match ad spend to campaigns by the ad-platform campaign ID.
text: What the cost sync does Meta Ads cost sync pulls each day's spend , impressions and clicks from Meta and folds the spend into the matching tracker campaign, so cost, profit and ROI line up without you typing daily budgets by hand. It runs on a schedule, off the tracking path, or on demand with Sync now . The spend it reads for a matched campaign and day is treated as authoritative for that day. There are two halves: connect the platform and choose your ad accounts once under Manage → Integrations , then switch the sync on and tune it under Settings → Meta Ads cost sync . Connect Meta under Integrations Open Manage → Integrations . The Ad platforms card lists Meta alongside placeholders for the other platforms. Press Connect on the Meta tile. The browser leaves the tracker, you authorise on Meta, and it returns to the Integrations page with a confirmation. Once connected, the tile shows Connected as … with the number of ad accounts and datasets discovered, and the expiry date of the connection. If the tile ever reads Needs reconnect , the stored token can no longer be read or has expired — press Connect again. Disconnect removes the connection and its stored token. Pick the ad account(s) With Meta connected, the tile shows Ad accounts for cost sync , a multi-select fed by the accounts discovered on your connection. Select every account whose spend you want tracked and press Save accounts . This is the only place accounts are chosen; the cost-sync card in Settings shows the saved list read-only, which is why it can look empty until you choose here. With no account selected, the sync has nothing to read. If the picker is empty, the connection exists but Meta returned no ad accounts for it — reconnect and grant access to the right business. Turn the sync on and set its cadence Open Settings → Meta Ads cost sync (under the ad-platform section) and switch on Keep my Meta costs up to date . Then set: Setting What it controls Test mode Work out the numbers and log them, but don't change any costs yet. On by default — nothing is written until you switch it off. How often The cadence: Hourly or Daily . Days to look back The backfill window, re-checked on every run. Default 7 ; set 0 for yesterday only. A wider window re-reads recent days, so late-published spend self-corrects. Match campaigns by How Meta campaigns are matched to yours: Auto — best match (recommended) , Meta campaign ID , Campaign name or Tracking ID (UTM / sub-id) . The last sync time, outcome, and the matched / unmatched counts are shown next to Sync now . A failed run records its error there rather than silently doing nothing. How spend is matched to a campaign Every Meta insight row carries a platform campaign id and name. The sync indexes your campaigns and matches in this order: the campaign's explicit Ad-platform campaign ID column, then the campaign name (case-insensitive), then the campaign's tracking id . Auto lets all three run in that order. Choosing one of the other values restricts matching to that single strategy, which is useful when names collide and you want the id to be the only truth. Set the Ad-platform campaign ID Open the campaign and find Ad-platform campaign ID on the Settings step. Its hint reads Meta Ads campaign id — used by the Meta Ads cost sync to match spend to this campaign . When a Meta connection exists, this is a picker fed by your discovered Meta campaigns; without one, you can type the id by hand. Leave it empty and the sync falls back to matching on name or tracking id, which is less reliable. Test mode and Sync now In Test mode the sync still makes the read-only request and computes every match, but writes no costs — the result panel shows exactly what it would have done. Use Sync now to run it on demand; the button respects test mode. Once you are happy with the matches, turn test mode off and run again to write the costs. Spend is spread across the matched campaign's clicks for that day. If a matched campaign-day had no tracker clicks, the daily figure is still stored for the audit trail but there is nothing to allocate. Transient network failures are retried with backoff before a run is marked failed. Test mode is on by default A fresh setup records runs and computes matches but never changes a cost. If your campaign cost stays at zero while the sync looks healthy, check that Test mode is off and that at least one ad account is selected under Integrations . If a cost is missing or wrong after a run, work through Cost is missing or wrong . For how costs are recorded in the first place — models, the cost parameter and per-click allocation — see Cost models and cost handling .

title: Landers and the landing editor
description: Upload landers, edit them in the landing editor, and route visitors between a landing page and an offer inside a flow.
text: What a lander is A lander (landing page) is an optional page that warms the visitor up before the offer. In a flow it sits between the incoming click and the click-out: the tracker serves your page, and a link on it sends the visitor on to the offer. Two flow schemas use landers — landing_offer serves a landing and then the offer, and landing_only serves the landing with no click-out. The multi schema can rotate one landing and one offer from pools. The Campaigns and flows page covers how a flow picks among them. Local vs external landers Every lander has a type. The difference is where the page actually comes from: Type Behaviour file (local file) An uploaded archive or single file, served from the tracker. This is the only type you can edit in the landing editor. link Redirects the visitor to an external landing URL. Nothing is hosted here. mirror Fetches an external URL server-side and re-serves it through the tracker. Use local when you want to host and edit the page, rewrite its assets and route its click-out through the tracker. Use link or mirror when the page already lives elsewhere and you only want to point at it. Uploading a lander Open Manage → Landers and press Create landing . On the Upload file tab, fill in the fields and attach the file: Folder name — lowercase letters, numbers and underscores only, up to 250 characters. The local lander is served at /l/ . Name and Tags — the internal label and free-form tags for filtering. Landing type — choose file . Landing file (.zip, .php, .html) — the upload itself. A .zip must contain an index.php or index.html at its root (not nested inside a subfolder). You can also upload a single .php or .html file. Grab from URL instead The Grab from URL tab fetches a page server-side and stores it as a local lander. A built-in guard accepts only http(s) URLs with publicly resolvable hosts and refuses localhost and internal addresses; tick Allow internal/private address (own infrastructure) only when grabbing from your own infrastructure behind the same proxy. A grabbed page is capped at 3 MB . Allowed file types and size caps Limit Value Upload file types .zip , .php , .html Files the editor accepts .html , .php , .css , .js , .jpg , .jpeg , .png Zip entries Up to 2000 files Single file inside a zip Up to 50 MB Total uncompressed archive Up to 200 MB , and no more than a 100:1 compression ratio Grabbed page Up to 3 MB The archive caps are checked before extraction, so an oversized or zip-bomb archive is refused rather than expanded. The landing editor Local landers can be edited in the built-in code editor. In the Landers list, open a row's Code editor action — it opens /backend/editor?landing={id} for that lander. The page has two panes: File tree (left). Every file and folder in the lander, so you can see the whole structure at a glance. Click a file to open it. Create file adds a new one by path (for example subdir/newfile.php ); Upload file drops an additional asset into the lander. Editor (right). Syntax-highlighted editing for HTML, CSS, JS and PHP. An Unsaved changes marker appears once you edit; Save writes the file back. Insert script splices a saved script from your library at the cursor or before / . The {offer} click-out macro Inside a local lander's HTML, the placeholder {offer} is replaced at serve time with the click-out URL /c/{alias}/{offer_id} . That URL carries the landing id, the click id and the mapped passthrough tokens automatically, so the tracker can attribute the click-out and then redirect to the offer. A button therefore looks like this: Continue Leave {offer} intact — if you replace it with a hard-coded destination, the click-out no longer passes through the tracker and the step loses its attribution. The offer's own URL is where the other macros ( {click_id} , {sub_id_1} , …) are placed; see Offers and offer URLs and Click IDs and URL macros . How a flow points at a lander, then an offer In the campaign wizard, give the flow a schema that uses landers — landing_offer to serve a page then the offer, or landing_only to serve the page alone. Attach the lander (or a pool of them under multi ). Attach the offer. The visitor loads the lander, and clicking its {offer} link hits /c/{alias}/{offer_id} , which redirects to the offer URL. Lander and offer are chosen per visitor, and with binding on a visitor keeps the same variant on return. The click-out that does not convert If click-outs show no conversions, check that the button still uses {offer} and that the archive had its index.html or index.php at the root. A hard-coded link skips the tracker; a nested index means the lander has no entry page to serve.

title: Domains and SSL
description: Point your own domain at campaigns and offers so links stay clean, with certificates handled for you.
text: What a tracking domain does A tracking domain is the address your campaign links, served landing pages and postback URL all answer on. When you build a campaign you choose which domain its link uses, and the link takes the form: https://<domain>/<alias> Add domains under Tools → Domains with Add domain . Each row stores the hostname, whether to Redirect to HTTPS , its 404 handling ( Handle 404 errors serves the tracker's styled page; Error returns a bare response), an optional Default campaign for visitors who reach / with no alias, and an optional group name. Add only a hostname you control, because you are about to point its DNS here. Add the DNS record The Domains page shows this tracker's public IP in its banner. You have two equivalent ways to point a hostname at it: Record Use it for Value A An apex or bare domain, such as example.com The server IP shown in the Domains banner CNAME A subdomain, such as track.example.com Your tracker host Use one record per hostname — you do not need both. A CNAME has the advantage that the tracker host's address can change without you editing DNS again. While DNS propagates Add the domain row first. It shows a pending status while it waits. Create the record at your DNS provider, using the value above. Allow time to propagate — usually minutes, but up to a day where a long TTL was cached. You can keep building campaigns and offers in the meantime; nothing is lost. Do not send live traffic to the domain yet. Until it resolves here and has a certificate, HTTPS will not work, so test on the tracker host or another live domain in the meantime. Check DNS Each row has a DNS check button. It looks the domain up and compares the answer with this server's address, then shows one of three states: Points here — the domain resolves to this tracker; you can issue a certificate. Resolves elsewhere — DNS answers, but not with this server. Usually a stale record, a proxy in front of it, or a record created at the wrong provider. No DNS — nothing resolves yet. Propagation has not finished, or the record is missing. The Check domains statuses button re-tests every domain over HTTP and updates the Status column. Update SSL Once DNS points here, use the row's Update SSL for 90 days action. The tracker confirms the domain over plain HTTP and issues the certificate automatically. This can take up to 10 minutes per domain , so keep the page open until it confirms. The SSL Status and SSL Expiry columns then show the state — a day count while it is valid, and warning , critical , expired or No cert when it is not. With Redirect to HTTPS on, plain-http requests for this domain are upgraded to https. Wildcards and renewal The certificate follows the domain row, so it covers the exact hostname you added. Add every hostname you actually serve — for example track.example.com and www.example.com — as its own row. One entry does not cover its subdomains, and a wildcard certificate is not part of this flow. Certificates are valid for 90 days and renewal is not automatic on every setup. Watch the SSL Expiry column and re-run Update SSL before it lapses, or enable the renewal timer on the host so it renews for you. A lapsed certificate breaks the HTTPS redirect for that domain, and links and postbacks that expect HTTPS start failing. Why hits land in the right workspace A domain belongs to exactly one workspace. On every click and every /pb postback the tracker reads the hostname the request arrived on, resolves the workspace that owns it, and then matches the campaign alias or click id strictly inside that workspace. Aliases are unique per workspace rather than globally, so two workspaces can each run a campaign called promo without colliding, as long as they are served on different domains. A request on a host that no workspace owns is refused rather than guessed, so a conversion can never be credited to the wrong workspace's numbers. This is also why the postback URL you give a network must use the same domain as the campaign link. Pointing it at a staging or old domain sends the call to a workspace you are not watching. See Postback not recorded . The certificate challenge runs over HTTP first A certificate can only be issued after the domain already routes here, because the check is fetched over plain HTTP. Confirm DNS and allow propagation before pressing Update SSL . One domain, many campaigns A single domain can serve any number of campaigns through their aliases and can carry a default campaign for bare / visits. Add a second domain when you want separate branding, or to keep an old link alive.

title: Reports, breakdowns and saved views
description: Read reports and breakdowns, edit or delete a conversion, and save the views you check every day.
text: Break down by any dimension Open Performance → Reports . The report builder turns your live click stream into a drill-down table. Choose a Date range , one or more Campaigns , and an ordered set of dimensions in the Breakdown pipeline , then press Run report . You can stack up to five dimensions . They read left to right, and clicking a value in the table expands the next level beneath it. Any of these can be a dimension: Time — date, hour, ISO week Objects — campaign, offer, landing page Geo — country, region, city Device — device type, OS, OS version, browser, language Traffic — traffic source, UTM source/medium/campaign/creative, keyword, ISP, connection type Identifiers — Sub ID 1 through Sub ID 10, domain, IP, user agent Quality — conversion status, bot flag, proxy flag Preset chains load in one click: SubID chain , Geo chain , Traffic chain and Funnel . The Report templates gallery loads a whole configuration — dimensions, columns and window — for common jobs such as campaign performance, offer/landing split or device breakdown. Metrics and date basis Columns include visits, unique visits, clicks, unique clicks, leads, conversions, rejected, cost, revenue, profit, and the derived CR %, EPC and ROI %, plus bot clicks, bot cost, fraud score average and human clicks. Pick the columns you want, sort by any of them, and use Custom metrics to add a formula over the built-in keys, for example conversions*100/clicks . The Click date / Conversion date toggle decides which timestamp the range filters on. Click date counts a conversion on the day its click happened; conversion date counts it on the day the conversion arrived. Compare the two when a network reports late. Saved views, presets and templates Three different things can be saved here, and they are not interchangeable: What Action What it stores Saved report Save report Dimensions, columns, custom metrics, date basis and filters — reload it from the Saved reports dropdown Column template Save as template Only which columns are visible in this table Filter preset Save filters Only the filter values currently applied Use as default pins the current columns as the workspace default for that table, so the next person opening it sees the same view. The conversion log Below the builder is the Conversion log — every conversion received via postback. Filter it by Status , Approval , a free-text Search (click id, external id, transaction id, visitor id) and Offer URL contains . Each row has an Edit action and a Delete action. Edit opens a dialog where you can change Status , Approval , Payout , Revenue , External ID and Transaction ID . This is how you correct a conversion a network reported late, or with the wrong status or amount. Select rows to apply a status or approval in bulk, and use Add conversion or Import for offline sales. Remember that a later postback still updates the row: status follows the latest event and payout accumulates, so a manual edit is not necessarily final. The read-only list of the same records lives at Logs → Conversions ; editing happens here. Exporting Export CSV appears on the report, the click log and the conversion log, and exports exactly what the current filters select. Every cell is quoted, so values always open as plain text and separators or newlines cannot break the rows. The separate Warehouse export card writes raw click, conversion and cost datasets with a manifest for BI tools, over its own date range and with optional gzip. Retroactive cost update When cost is missing or wrong for a period, an admin can correct it without re-importing anything. Press Cost update and choose an optional Campaign (leave it empty for all campaigns), a From and To date, and a Cost per click . The tracker overwrites the per-click cost on every matching row, so total spend is cost × matched rows and existing costs are replaced rather than added. A cost of 0 clears costs for the window. Every change is recorded in Logs → Cost updates with who ran it and how many rows changed. See also Cost models and cost handling . Sharing a report Save a report, then use its Share report action to create a tokenized public link. Anyone with the link — a client or a partner — sees a clean read-only copy of that one breakdown, with no login required. Revoking the link or re-creating it invalidates the old one instantly. A saved report can also be emailed on a schedule with Email schedule . A capped report shows short totals A breakdown returns at most 1,000 rows. When that cap is reached the table says so, and the totals only cover the rows shown. Narrow the date range or campaigns, add a filter, or use fewer dimensions to see every row.

title: Logs: what each one shows
description: What the clicks, conversions, S2S postbacks and internal postbacks logs each show, and when to open which one.
text: Six trails, one shape The Logs section keeps six separate event trails, one per sidebar entry. Every page has the same controls: a From and To date range, filters for that log, Refresh , Export CSV , a Columns picker and a Preset dropdown where you can Save filters and reuse them later. A log can also be opened pre-filtered by a link. Put a filter name in the query string — for example ?click_id=YOUR-CLICK-ID — and the matching field is filled in when the page loads. The Health centre uses this to jump from a failed delivery straight to the row behind it. Copy a click id from Logs → Clicks and paste it into any other log's URL to follow one visitor across all six. Clicks Every click the tracker received. Columns: Time , Click id , IP , Country , Device , Status , URL , Bot . Filters: Country , Device , OS , Status , and a free-text Search over URL, IP and visitor id. Open it when you need to confirm a click actually arrived — a campaign link hit lands here first — or to copy a click id for a manual postback test. The Bot flag tells you at a glance whether the hit was filtered as automated. Conversions The inbound conversion records as stored. Columns: Time , Click id , Status , Campaign , Offer , Payout , Revenue , Transaction . Filters: Status , Click id and Campaign id . Open it when a postback returned 200 and you want to see the conversion row it created, or to confirm that an unknown click id became an unattributed row. This list is read-only; to change a status, payout or delete a row, use the conversion log on Reports . S2S postbacks Every inbound server-to-server call to /pb , accepted or not.
