Columns: Time , Click id , Status , Result , Payout , Transaction , Source IP , Reason , Raw URL . Filters: Click id , Status , Result , and a free-text Search over URL, reason and IP. The Result column is the diagnosis: accepted , duplicate , rejected or a rule/block outcome, with the Reason spelling out why. Open it when a network says it posted but revenue did not move — the reason tells you whether the call was refused before anything was written, or removed by the duplicate guard. See Postback not recorded . Internal postbacks The outbound delivery attempts this tracker sent onward, such as conversions pushed to an ad platform. Columns: Time , Click id , Platform , Pixel , Event , Status , HTTP , Outcome , Attempts , Response . Filters: Click id , Event , Conversion status and Outcome . The HTTP column and the clipped Response body are the delivery receipt: they show what the receiving platform answered. Open it when a conversion is missing downstream — the tracker recorded it, but the send may have failed or been retried. See Sending conversions to Meta (CAPI) for one platform's path. Click forwarding Every redirect decision a click went through. Columns: Time , Click id , Campaign , Flow , Schema , Offer , Status , Destination , Reason . Filters: Click id , Campaign id , Status , and a free-text Search over reason and destination. Open it when a visitor reached the wrong destination or no redirect at all. The Status and Reason show which routing outcome was taken — a normal redirect, a fallback, a cap, an out-of-schedule flow or a blocked request — and the Destination is the URL the visitor was sent to. Cost updates Retroactive cost changes applied from Reports . Columns: Time , Username , Campaign , From , To , Cost , Rows . Filters: Username and Campaign id . Open it when cost for a period changed unexpectedly or you want to know who last touched it. Each row records who applied the update, the window it covered, the new per-click cost and how many rows were rewritten. Follow one click across every log Copy the click id from Logs → Clicks , then open another log with ?click_id=… appended to its URL. The filter is seeded for you, so Clicks → Click forwarding → S2S postbacks → Internal postbacks read as one story.

title: Health centre and system status
description: Watch failed outbound sends, the last successful postback per source, and the public system status page.
text: What the Health centre is Open Tools → Health centre for a single read of everything the tracker can honestly say about itself: whether its stores answer, how its background loops are keeping time, what failed to send out in the last day, and which traffic sources have gone quiet. For clicks, conversions and profit, use Reports and the logs . It reads live state on load and again whenever you press Re-check . It is part of the workspace management plane, visible to owners and admins by default and grantable per section. The verdict banner At the top sits one verdict: All clear when nothing is wrong, or Attention needed when anything below is flagged. The banner agrees with the incident console underneath — if the console has any row at all, the verdict will not claim all clear. Under the headline, a short list spells out the summary reasons (a store not answering, a stale loop, a run of failed sends). Incident console The console groups every finding the page can derive into three severities. Each row names the subject and its area, gives the reason, and offers a fix link that jumps to the page where it is resolved. Severity Typical examples Critical The main database is not answering; the analytics store is not answering; a domain's TLS certificate has expired or expires within 7 days; an integration token already expired. Warning A background loop is stale; more than a handful of outbound sends failed in 24 hours; a source has not delivered an accepted postback in more than 7 days; a domain does not resolve; a stored integration token expires within 7 days. Info A domain resolves but not to this server's address (a proxy or CDN in front is legitimate); a certificate could not be read. When the console is empty it shows a green No incidents state — every check this backend can make came back clean. Databases Two rows report reachability and a small round-trip latency: Database — the primary store; the row reads reachable with a millisecond round-trip, or unreachable . Analytics — the store that serves the click stream; shown the same way. A store that does not answer becomes a critical incident, since the numbers elsewhere depend on it. Background loops The tracker runs several loops on its own schedule. The Health centre lists each one with its cadence, its last run, and a state chip: Loop Cadence What it does Monitor 15 min Probes active campaigns' flow URLs and can auto-disable a flow after repeated failures. Auto rules 15 min Evaluates your automation rules and fires their actions (pause, alert). Optimizer 15 min Re-weights flows for campaigns with the optimizer enabled. Insights 15 min Runs the anomaly detectors and alerts on new critical findings. Meta cost sync periodic Pulls ad spend from the connected ad platform. The state chip is ok , stale , or not yet run . A loop that has not had its first pass since the process started is not yet run , not stale — normal after a restart and not an incident. A loop whose heartbeat is far older than its cadence is stale and appears in the incident console with its age in minutes. Failed outbound sends (24h) The Process card shows the app version, its uptime, and a count of Failed outbound sends (24h) — conversions the tracker tried to deliver onward to an ad platform and could not. A few are noise; a burst is worth acting on and will surface both in the attention list and as a warning incident linking to Manage → CAPI integrations . Last successful postback per source The last card is the quickest way to tell whether an affiliate network has gone quiet. It lists one row per traffic source with the timestamp of that source's most recent accepted inbound postback, newest first. The source name is a link that opens Logs → S2S postbacks already filtered to that postback's click id, so you can see the exact call. Only accepted postbacks from the last 30 days are considered; a source with none shows an empty state instead of a row. A source with no accepted postback for more than 7 days is called out as a warning incident. Counts and totals A row of tiles summarizes the workspace: clicks, conversions, campaigns, users, postbacks and CAPI attempts. They are scope indicators, not a report — for a date range or a breakdown, go to Reports. The System status card The Documentation page has a second tab, System status , shown to workspace managers. It is a lighter version of the same idea and it refreshes itself every 15 seconds: a Version tile, plus Database and Analytics tiles that read Up with a latency in milliseconds or Down ; Clicks (24h) and Conversions (24h) tiles, so you can see at a glance whether events are still flowing; a Background loops table with each loop's last run, marked not yet when it has not run since boot; a footer line with the app version and the polling interval, and the landings disk's used and free space where that is reported. What this page cannot see The Health centre reports only from inside the application — the reachability of its own stores, its own loops, its own outbound sends. It does not inspect the host or its containers, so "All clear" means every check the app can make passed, not that the whole server is healthy.

title: Team members, invitations and roles
description: Invite teammates, assign roles and understand who can see or change what inside a workspace.
text: Where team management lives Open Account → Users . The page has three parts: Workspace members , Pending invitations (sent but not yet accepted), and — for platform operators only — a Platform users card for install-wide accounts. The workspace card shows your plan and seats used, for example Seats used: 4 / 10 or (unlimited) when no limit is set. Managing members is an owners-and-admins job. An editor or viewer sees the member list read-only: the Invite member and Add existing user buttons are disabled, and role selectors are not shown. The four roles A membership carries exactly one role. The role decides what the person can reach inside this workspace: Role What it can reach owner Everything in the workspace, including ownership. The owner can transfer ownership and is the only role that can promote another member to owner. A workspace has one owner. admin Everything in the workspace except changing the owner. Admins manage members, invitations and settings. This is the role that sees the full management area. editor Read and write on the content sections — campaigns, offers, landings, sources and the like. No management plane: Users and the workspace settings are out of reach by default. viewer Read-only across the content sections. Can look, cannot change. Ownership is never assigned through the ordinary role picker. To move it, use the crown action on a member row — Make owner via Transfer ownership . The target is promoted and you step down to admin. The last owner of a workspace can never be demoted or removed. Invite a member Invite member is how a new person joins. The dialog takes an email, a username, or both — provide at least one — and a role. When you send it, the invitee is emailed a link that opens the sign-in page in an invite state, where they choose a username and a password (at least 8 characters) and create their own account. They are then signed in and added to the workspace with the role you chose. Press Invite member on the Workspace members card. Enter the invitee's Email and/or Username , and pick a Role . Press Send invitation . If the email goes out, the result dialog confirms it; if it does not, copy the link and pass it on by hand. Copy the Invitation link (or the raw Token ) while the dialog is open — it is shown only once. Two limits apply. Each invitation is single-use and expires after 7 days , and a role ceiling stops you inviting above your own role: an owner can invite any role including owner, while an admin tops out at admin. Add an existing user Add existing user attaches an account that already exists to this workspace. It takes a Username and a Role and does not email anyone. Because it grants workspace access without the person's consent, it is deliberately narrow: an existing account can only be attached when it already belongs to this workspace's own hierarchy. An unrelated account is refused and must be brought in through the invitation flow instead, and a platform operator's account can never be added to a workspace this way. Use Invite member when the person is new or lives in a different workspace. Pending invitations and revoking them The Pending invitations card lists every invitation that has been sent and neither accepted nor expired, with its invitee, role, inviter and expiry date. Press the red Revoke action on a row to cancel it — the link stops working immediately. Revoking an invitation does not affect an account that has already accepted one; remove that member instead. Seat limits The workspace's plan sets a seat count. The member card shows seats used against the limit, and when every seat is taken the add and invite actions are refused with a clear message — for example Workspace seat limit reached (10 of 10 seats used) . A plan with no seat count is unlimited. Seats are counted from the current members, not from outstanding invitations. Per-section permissions Behind the role is a permission map. Its defaults are exactly the role table above: owners and admins get every section and write access; editors get the content sections with write access; viewers get the content sections read-only. The management sections — Users and Settings among them — are off for editors and viewers unless explicitly granted. A membership can override the defaults section by section, switch the global write flag, and apply two further restrictions: Owner scope — for campaigns, offers, sources, affiliates and domains, a section can be set to Own only , so the person sees and edits just the rows they own. Everything else is hidden from their pickers and refused if requested directly. All keeps full access. Hidden metrics — cost, revenue, profit, ROI and other chosen metrics can be removed from a user's view. The restriction is enforced server-side: the values are stripped from responses, breakdowns, logs and CSV exports alike, not merely hidden in the interface. Workspace admin vs platform operator A workspace admin manages this workspace — its members, invitations and settings — and sees the management area inside it. That is separate from platform account management , which lives on the install-wide Platform users card and is shown only to platform operators. Platform operators create, activate, disable and delete the global accounts, reset another user's two-factor authentication and inspect any user's devices; workspace managers do not touch that plane.

title: Password, two-factor and sessions
description: Change your password, turn on two-factor authentication and review the sessions signed in to your account.
text: Change your password Open the account menu in the top bar and choose Change password . The dialog asks for three values: Current password — proving it is you; the change is refused without it. New password — the field label reads New password (min 8 chars) . Everywhere a password is set — here, the invitation form and the reset form — the minimum is 8 characters . Repeat new password — must match the new one. Press Change and the new password is live on your next sign-in. Changing your password this way does not sign your other devices out — sessions stay valid until they expire or you revoke them. If you want devices signed out as well, use the sessions card described below, or the reset flow. Forgot your password On the sign-in page, follow Forgot password? . Enter your Username or email and press Email me a reset link . The tracker answers the same way whether or not the account exists, so the page cannot be used to discover which accounts are real, and it emails a link only when there is a matching account with an address. If nothing arrives, check that the account has an email on file. The email carries a link that opens the sign-in page in a reset state, asking for a New password and a confirmation. The link is single-use and expires after 60 minutes ; a fresh request spends any earlier outstanding links. A completed reset requires at least 8 characters. What a reset does to your sessions A password reset is a security event: setting a new password through the emailed link signs every session on the account out, including any you had open on other devices. You then sign in again with the new password. This is the difference worth remembering — Change password leaves other sessions running; a forgot-password reset ends them all. The thing readers get wrong People use "reset my password" when they mean "change my password", and are surprised to be logged out everywhere. Use Change password when you know the current one and want to stay signed in; use the forgot-password link when you do not, and expect to sign in again on every device. Set up two-factor authentication Open the account menu and choose Two-factor authentication . With 2FA off, press Set up 2FA and the dialog walks you through it: Scan the QR code with an authenticator app, or copy the secret shown beside it and enter it manually. Type the 6-digit verification code the app generates. Press Enable 2FA . On success you are shown 10 backup codes . They are displayed only once , so save them somewhere safe now. Each backup code is a single-use, 8-character code (the alphabet avoids 0 , O , 1 and I ), and each works exactly once — in place of, not in addition to, a normal code. Signing in with 2FA After your username and password are accepted, the sign-in page asks for a code. Enter the current 6-digit authenticator code , or one of your backup codes . The authenticator code is accepted within a small ±1 time-step window, so a code from the neighbouring 30-second slot still works. If you have lost your authenticator and your backup codes, a platform operator can reset 2FA for the account so you can sign in with a password and set it up again. Disabling 2FA Open the same dialog; with 2FA enabled it shows the enabled state and a Disable 2FA button. Disabling requires your password, and it clears the secret and the backup codes. View and revoke active sessions Open Account → Users and find the Active sessions card. It lists the devices currently signed in to your account, newest first, with the device type, operating system, browser, IP, location, when each was last seen and when it started. The row for the device you are using now is tagged This device . Revoke one session — press the red revoke action on any row that is not the current device. That device is signed out immediately. Log out all other devices — the button above the table ends every session except the one you are using, and reports how many it revoked. The current device cannot be revoked from this list — use Logout in the account menu when you want to end it. Location comes from the proxy or CDN geo information attached to the request; where none is present the location stays blank rather than being guessed. Platform operators can additionally open another user's Devices list from the Platform users card. If you think an account is compromised Reset the password through the forgot-password flow — that signs every session out at once — then sign back in, turn on two-factor authentication, and review Active sessions for anything you do not recognise. Security-relevant changes such as 2FA enable, disable and resets are recorded in the audit log under Settings → Audit log .

title: Securing your postback URL
description: Lock down the inbound postback URL with a secret key and an IP allowlist, and understand what a 403 response means.
text: Why an open postback URL can be abused Your inbound postback endpoint, https://YOUR-TRACKER-DOMAIN/pb , has to be reachable by every affiliate network you work with. That also means it is reachable by anyone else who learns the URL. An attacker who knows a valid click id — or who can guess one — can post a fabricated conversion and quietly change your numbers: Padding revenue. Fake sale postbacks inflate payout and revenue, which flatters ROI, EPC and every report that reads them. Hiding bad traffic. A stream of fake lead conversions can mask a source that is really underperforming. Polluting attribution. Junk conversions tie themselves to real clicks and distort which campaign, offer or creative looks profitable. The endpoint is public by design, so the fix is not to hide it but to require proof that a caller is allowed to use it. The two controls Both live in Settings → Postback security . Turn the panel on with the switch Require a secret key or IP allowlist for inbound postbacks , then fill either or both fields. When the panel is enabled, a postback must satisfy every non-empty check . If you enable it and leave both fields empty, postbacks are still allowed — so set at least one. Control Field What it enforces Secret key Secret key Every postback must carry a matching key, or it is refused. IP allowlist Allowed IPs Only callers whose source IP is listed may post. Accepts a comma-separated list of IPs and CIDR ranges, for example 203.0.113.5, 10.0.0.0/8 . Use the key alone when a network posts from a range that changes; add the allowlist when the network can give you a stable set of sending addresses. How the key travels The key is accepted in three places, so you can fit whichever shape a network's postback template supports: a ?key= query parameter, a ?secret= query parameter, an X-Postback-Key request header. For a URL-shaped template, append the key to the postback URL you hand the network: https://YOUR-TRACKER-DOMAIN/pb?clickid={clickid}&payout={payout}&status={status}&key=YOUR-SECRET If the network allows custom headers instead, keep the URL clean and pass the same value as X-Postback-Key . Either form works; do not put the key in both. The exact 403 a blocked postback gets A postback that fails either check is refused before it is read . It gets HTTP 403 with a JSON body naming the reason: {"detail":"Invalid or missing postback key"} An IP failure reads instead: {"detail":"Client IP '203.0.113.9' is not in the allowlist"} The attempt is also written to Logs → S2S postbacks with the result blocked and the same reason, so you can see which control refused it. Note that the check happens after the click id and payout are parsed but before any conversion is recorded — a blocked postback never becomes a conversion. Test it with curl Use a real click id from Logs → Clicks , then call the endpoint with and without the key: # with the key — accepted curl "https://YOUR-TRACKER-DOMAIN/pb?clickid=YOUR-CLICK-ID&payout=25&status=sale&key=YOUR-SECRET" # without the key — 403 curl -i "https://YOUR-TRACKER-DOMAIN/pb?clickid=YOUR-CLICK-ID&payout=25&status=sale" Or send the header instead of the query parameter: curl -H "X-Postback-Key: YOUR-SECRET" "https://YOUR-TRACKER-DOMAIN/pb?clickid=YOUR-CLICK-ID&payout=25&status=sale" A correct call answers 200 with {"status":"ok",…} . A blocked one answers 403 as above. Testing an IP allowlist from your own machine is less direct: your address must be the one the tracker sees, which may be a proxy in front of the network. Enable it before you hand the URL over Turn on the key before you paste the postback URL into a network's settings. The key then travels inside the URL the network stores, so there is nothing to re-edit later. Adding a key after a network is already live means every postback fails with a 403 until you update that network's template too. Keep the key, watch the logs Treat the secret like any credential: give a different value per workspace, rotate it if it leaks, and update the networks in the same sitting. After any change, watch Logs → S2S postbacks for a blocked result — it is the fastest signal that a network is still sending the old value.

title: Postback not recorded (400 / 403 / no match)
description: Diagnose a postback that never landed: 400 and 403 responses, click ids that do not match, and where to confirm what arrived.
text: First, confirm what the network sent Before changing anything, open Logs → S2S postbacks . Every inbound call is listed there, whether it was accepted or rejected, so the log tells you which of the cases below you are actually in. If the call is not there at all, the problem is on the network's side or in the URL you gave it — not in your parameter mapping. 400 — invalid status or payout A 400 means the tracker understood the call but refused the values. There are just two common causes: Unknown status. The status the network sent is not one of lead , sale , upsale , rejected , hold , trash , and is not a custom status you have defined. Check the spelling the network uses and either map it in the network's postback template or define the status in Settings. Non-numeric payout. The payout value contains a currency symbol, a comma decimal separator, or text. Send a plain number — the currency is not part of the payout and is not accepted on this endpoint. Remember the aliases: if the network sends type instead of status , or sum instead of payout , that is fine and does not cause a 400. An empty status defaults to lead , and an empty payout to 0 — those are not errors either. 403 — postback security A 403 means the call was blocked before it was read. Two controls can block it, both under Settings → Postback security : Secret key. You have required a key, and the network did not send it. The key can travel as ?key= , ?secret= , or the X-Postback-Key header. Add it to the postback URL you gave the network, or remove the requirement. IP allowlist. You have restricted callers to a list of IPs or CIDR ranges, and the network's server is not on it. Networks frequently send from a range that changes; if you cannot pin it down, either widen the allowlist or turn the IP check off and rely on the secret key instead. If a mirror or a proxy sits between the network and the tracker, the address the tracker sees may be the proxy's, not the network's. 200 but no conversion appears If the log shows a 200 and the response was {"status":"ok",…} , the conversion was recorded. If you cannot see it, you are usually looking at the wrong click. The click id does not match The most common cause is that the click id never made it round the loop. The tracker appends click_id=… to the offer URL automatically, but almost every network reads its own parameter. If you did not add that parameter to the offer's Target URL — for example &sub1={click_id} — the network has nothing to send back, and the postback arrives with an empty or wrong click id. To confirm: open Logs → Clicks , copy a recent click id, and post it by hand. A {"status":"ok",…} answers whether the endpoint works; then compare that click id with the one your network is actually sending. It matched, but not the click you expected When the click id cannot be matched, the tracker falls back to the transaction id , then to unique sub-ids within its window, then records an unattributed row. If your network sends an old or reused transaction id, the fallback can attach the conversion somewhere unexpected. Check the conversion in Reports → Conversions and delete or correct it from there. Nothing arrived at all Wrong URL shape. The endpoint is https://YOUR-TRACKER-DOMAIN/pb . If you pasted the legacy path form, it redirects, but a network that does not follow redirects will see nothing. Wrong domain. The postback URL must point at the same tracker domain your campaign link uses. A staging or old domain will accept the call into a place you are not looking. The network only fires on certain statuses. Many networks send a postback for approved sales only. A pending or rejected conversion may simply never be reported. The network is quiet. Health centre shows the last successful postback per source; if it stopped at a specific time, the problem is on the network side. A checklist Open Logs → S2S postbacks and find the call. If 400 — fix the status name or send a plain numeric payout. If 403 — fix the key in the URL, or the IP allowlist. If 200 — open Logs → Clicks , fire a known click id by hand, and compare. Confirm the offer's Target URL carries the network's own click-id parameter (for example &sub1={click_id} ). Confirm the postback URL points at your live tracker domain and uses the /pb?… query form. The manual test There is no test-postback button. Fire a click on the campaign link, copy the click id from Logs → Clicks , then call /pb with curl. That exercises the same path a network uses and rules the endpoint in or out immediately.

title: Meta shows no conversions
description: Why Meta shows no conversions, and how to check the outbound send to the ad platform without leaving the tracker.
text: Work the checks in order “Meta shows no conversions” almost always means the tracker recorded the conversion, but the outbound send to Meta never ran or was refused. Work the checks in order — each rules out a class of cause before the next. Every send attempt is visible in Logs → Internal postbacks , so several answers are on one screen. 1. Is dry-run still on? This is the most common cause, and it is easy to forget. On Manage → CAPI integrations , open Meta . The switch Dry-run (build + log the payload, send nothing) is on by default — a fresh setup never sends anything until you turn it off. With dry-run on, the event is built and audited but no HTTP request leaves the tracker. In Logs → Internal postbacks the outcome is dry_run . Turn the switch off and save. 2. Did the click carry an fbclid? Meta matches a server-side event back to the ad click using click identifiers, not the tracker's click id. The tracker captures fbclid from the ad URL automatically and stitches it with the _fbc and _fbp cookies — you do not map it. Check the click: open Logs → Clicks , find a recent click from your Meta campaign, and look at its URL — it should contain fbclid= . A redirect, a landing page or a URL-builder that strips query parameters can drop it. In the conversion record, the derived values are fbc ( fb.1.<timestamp>.<fbclid> ) and fbp . If both are empty, the click arrived without them. 3. Is the dataset/pixel id and token correct? On the Meta panel in Manage → CAPI integrations , the id and the token must belong together and to the right dataset: Fallback Dataset / Pixel ID and Fallback access token apply when no pixel record is bound. If you use pixel records, each has a Pixel / Dataset ID and an API key / Access token , and must be bound to a traffic channel or an offer. A wrong pair fails authentication at Meta and lands in Internal postbacks as outcome failed , with a non-2xx HTTP code and Meta's error text in Response . An id with no bound pixel yields not_configured . Use Send test event to validate credentials directly. 4. Is the conversion's status in the list you send? The panel has a row of checkboxes, Send these conversion statuses . If the conversion's status is not ticked, the send is skipped silently — the event never reaches Meta and no row appears in Internal postbacks. The defaults are lead , sale and upsale . Also confirm the status has an event name. The tracker maps statuses to Meta events (for example sale → Purchase ). With pixel records, the pixel's Default event name applies unless a Custom conversion matching row overrides it. A status that is sent but maps to no event is skipped before a request is made. 5. Did a duplicate get suppressed? A send is claimed once per click id + status . If the same conversion is processed again — a repeated postback, a retried delivery — the duplicate is suppressed and nothing is sent. Like the status gate, a suppressed duplicate writes no row to Internal postbacks. That is normal and not a fault: if the first send succeeded, Meta already has the event. Do not confuse this with inbound de-duplication at /pb , which suppresses a repeated transaction id or an identical anonymous status + payout within about 60 seconds. Both mean “already handled”, not “lost”. 6. Is a test event code set? If Test event code is filled in on the Meta panel, every event is routed to the Test Events tab of Meta's Events Manager instead of the normal event stream. Events sent with a test code do not appear as conversions in your ad reporting. If you set one while testing, clear it and save — otherwise sends look successful while Meta's main view stays quiet. 7. Read Logs → Internal postbacks This is the outbound audit and the final word. Open Logs → Internal postbacks and look at the newest rows. The columns are Time , Click id , Platform , Pixel , Event , Status , HTTP , Outcome , Attempts and Response . Outcome What it means Where to look next sent Meta accepted the event (2xx). Matching, not delivery — check the click's fbc / fbp . failed Meta refused it; read Response . Usually token, dataset or payload — fix per the error text. dry_run Built and logged, nothing sent. Turn off dry-run. not_configured No usable dataset id or token. Fill the fallback fields or bind a pixel. not_implemented The pixel belongs to a platform whose sender is not live. Only Meta sends events today. Transient failures — a network error, 429 or 5xx — are retried up to three times; Attempts shows how many tries it took. A 4xx is terminal. If you see no row at all, recheck steps 1, 4 and 5 — a skipped send writes none. Fire a known conversion to compare To exercise the whole path deliberately, fire a postback for a real click from your Meta campaign. Copy the click id from Logs → Clicks , then: curl "https://YOUR-TRACKER-DOMAIN/pb?clickid=YOUR-CLICK-ID&payout=25&status=sale" A 200 with {"status":"ok",…} means the conversion was recorded; the tracker then queues the Meta send in the background. Watch Logs → Internal postbacks a moment later for the outbound result. The CAPI integration page covers each setting in full. “No row” is not “no attempt” A send skipped by dry-run, status filtering or duplicate suppression leaves no Internal postbacks row. Before assuming the sender is broken, confirm dry-run is off and the status is ticked — those two account for most silent cases.

title: Cost is missing or wrong
description: Fix a missing or wrong cost: check the cost model, the cost parameter on the campaign link, and the ad-platform sync.
text: How cost reaches a report Cost can arrive from three places, and a wrong number is usually a mismatch between them. Per-click cost comes from the cost parameter on the campaign link, or from the campaign's configured cost; synced spend comes from an ad platform; and a manual correction can be applied retroactively in Reports. Work the checks in order to find which of these is missing or feeding the wrong value. 1. Is there an Ad-platform campaign ID on the campaign? Cost sync matches a platform's spend to your campaign by id first. Open Manage → Campaigns , edit the campaign, and set Ad-platform campaign ID — for Meta this is the Meta Ads campaign id. Without it the sync falls back to matching by campaign name, then by the campaign's configured tracking identifiers; if none match, the platform's spend for that campaign is never attached and the campaign shows no synced cost. If Meta is connected, the field offers discovered campaigns to pick from, so copy the id from there rather than typing it. 2. Is Meta connected, and is the ad account selected? Cost sync has two switches outside the campaign. Open Manage → Integrations and check the Meta tile shows connected . Then, in the Ad accounts for cost sync picker on that tile, choose the ad accounts whose spend you want read, and press Save accounts . A connected platform with no account selected syncs nothing. If the tile reads Needs reconnect , the stored token can no longer be read or has expired — reconnect before looking at anything else. 3. Has the backfill window reached the day? The sync does not walk your whole history. It queries a rolling window ending today, going back a fixed number of days — by default 7 . A day older than that window is never re-fetched, so its spend stays at whatever was last written, or at zero if the campaign was created after the day passed. The tell is a cost that is correct for recent days and missing for older ones. Wait for the next scheduled run (the sync runs on a cadence, hourly or daily) and confirm the day is inside the window; if you need older days, widen the backfill window and re-run. 4. Currency mismatch This is the check people skip, and it makes a correct-looking cost read wrong. Spend is stored in the currency the ad platform reports for that ad account. Three currencies can be in play: the ad account's currency, which is what the platform returns; the campaign's Cost currency field (Manage → Campaigns); the workspace base currency from Settings → Multi-currency , which reports convert to before aggregating. If the campaign's Cost currency does not match the currency of the spend you are comparing it to, the figures will not line up. Multi-currency converts revenue, cost and payout into the single base currency, so once set, check that the ad account and base currency are on the same page. There is no currency parameter on /pb — a postback never sets currency; it comes from the offer or workspace. 5. Manual campaign cost versus synced spend Two mechanisms can both write per-click cost, and the last writer wins per campaign and day: Source When it applies Behaviour cost parameter on the campaign link Campaign has Cost from cost parameter on; the source maps its token to cost . Stored on the individual click; falls back to the campaign's Cost value for the whole period otherwise. Synced platform spend Campaign matched by Ad-platform campaign ID. Authoritative for that campaign and day; re-running a day replaces it (never adds), so re-syncs are idempotent. The campaign's Cost model ( CPC , CPUC , CPM , CPA , CPS , RevShare , Auto ) and its Cost value define the manual fallback. If a campaign has a stale manual cost, the sync overwrites it for any day it matches — so check whether the number you are seeing predates the last sync run. 6. The retroactive cost update in Reports For a correction the sync cannot make — an unmapped campaign or a one-off fix — open Performance → Reports and use the Cost update action. The Retroactive cost update dialog sets per-click cost on every matching analytics row: Choose a Campaign , or leave it empty to apply to all campaigns. Set the From and To dates for the window. Enter Cost per click and press Apply . Total spend becomes cost × matched rows, and existing costs are overwritten, not adjusted . Enter 0 to clear cost from a window. Each run is recorded in Logs → Cost updates with the user, campaign, date range, cost and number of rows changed. Correcting one day does not stick if the sync still covers it The last writer wins per campaign and day. A manual retroactive update is overwritten the next time the platform sync covers that same day. Fix the mapping or the campaign id first, or the manual correction will be replaced. Confirm where a number came from Logs → Cost updates shows manual edits. To see a per-click value actually recorded on traffic, check Logs → Clicks . Comparing the two tells you quickly whether the figure you are disputing came from a manual update or from the sync.
